Ibn al-Jawzi, al-Mawardi and al-Qurtubi report that the sura is Meccan, with possibly one verse, 'He who imposed the Qur'an upon you', revealed at al-Juhfa during the migration according to Ibn 'Abbas, while al-Hasan, 'Ata' and 'Ikrima hold the whole sura to be Meccan. Al-Sam'ani and al-Baghawi explain that the word 'believe' means to affirm and to accept the book as true.

This verse describes Pharaoh's conduct in the land of Egypt. He exalted himself with arrogance and tyranny, and he split the people into rival groups, using some of them to serve his rule. He oppressed one group, the Children of Israel, slaughtering their sons and sparing their women for service and humiliation. The verse ends by saying he was one of the corrupters. The commentators broadly agree on the general meaning. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Zamakhshari explain that 'exalted' means proud and domineering, that 'the land' means Egypt, that the 'sects' are groups or categories assigned different tasks, and that the oppressed group is the Children of Israel, whose subjugation meant enslavement. Ibn Kathir, al-Qurtubi and Ibn al-Jawzi note that dividing the people this way was a policy of divide and rule. On the reason for killing the sons, the accounts differ. Qatada, al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi report that a soothsayer told Pharaoh that a boy among the Children of Israel would end his kingdom; al-Suddi reports a dream of fire from Jerusalem that burned the Copts but spared the Israelites. Al-Razi cites these explanations and finds one more convincing than the others, without firmly rejecting the rest. Al-Zajjaj and al-Zamakhshari argue that if the soothsayer was right the killing could not prevent what was fated, and if he was wrong the killing had no purpose. Ibn 'Ashur and Ibn Sa'di read it as a policy to weaken the people by removing their men. For them, 'corruption' covers tyranny, unjust killing and the humiliation of the weak. The commentators do not settle between these explanations.

This verse states that God wishes to show favour to the Children of Israel, whom Pharaoh had reduced to weakness in the land of Egypt. He wills to make them leaders and rulers, and to make them heirs to Pharaoh and his people after their destruction, and to establish them in the land. The commentators recall that Pharaoh had exalted himself in the land, divided its people into factions, and slaughtered the sons of the Israelites while sparing their women, fearing a child who would end his rule. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Qurtubi agree that the Children of Israel are meant here, and that imamate means leadership and command in good; Mujahid adds calling people to good, while al-Dahhak understands the prophets. They differ on the heirs: al-Dahhak says they enslaved the Copts after Pharaoh drowned, others say they took the land and dwellings of Pharaoh, and Ibn 'Atiyya and Ibn Kathir take inheritance to mean succession over the earth. Al-Tabari and al-Baghawi note the readers' difference between the forms "nuriya" and "yara", with closely related meanings. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi explain that the verb expresses a past situation narrated, and that a favour close to fulfilment may be treated as contemporaneous with the oppression. Ibn Kathir reports that the Copts had learned of this child through Abraham. Ibn Sa'di sees a divine law covering any weak people who uphold the truth, and al-Shinqiti notes that patience and certainty are the basis of leadership according to other verses.

This verse belongs to the account of Moses and Pharaoh and announces God's promise to those who were oppressed in the land. The commentators explain that these are the Children of Israel, whom God wished to favour by delivering them, making them leaders in goodness and heirs to the rule of Pharaoh and his people, and establishing them in the land of Egypt and Syria. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir relate that Pharaoh, Haman and their armies then saw what they had feared: the loss of their kingdom at the hands of a man from the Children of Israel, which had driven them to slaughter the boys and spare the girls. The scholars agree that this establishment and inheritance were God's work alone, without any cause on the part of the Children of Israel, and that caution cannot avert what God has decreed. The meaning of "imams" varies: Ibn Abbas, Ibn Kathir and Mujahid take it as guides to good, Qatada as rulers and kings, and al-Dahhak as prophets. On the heirs, al-Dahhak says they enslaved the Copts after Pharaoh drowned, while others take it as inheriting the lands, homes and wealth, and a view reported by al-Mawardi from Ali identifies them as Joseph and his offspring. The reading "wa yara" in the third person differs from "wa nuri" in the first; al-Tabari judges both readings to have closely similar meanings. Ibn Ashur explains that inheritance here means succession to power and that Haman is more likely a title for a vizier than a proper name.

This passage records God's command to Moses' mother to nurse her son, to cast him into the river if she fears for him, and His promise that He will return him to her and make him one of the messengers. The commentators agree that this revelation was not prophethood, since she was not a prophetess, but they differ on its form. Qatada and Ibn 'Abbas took it as an inspiration cast into her heart, Mujahid placed the command to nurse before the birth while others placed it after, some spoke of a dream, and Qutrub and Muqatil of an angel sent to her. Ibn Kathir and Abu Hayyan judged that an inspiration or an angelic message is the most apparent reading. The fear mentioned is for the most part the fear of the slaughter Pharaoh ordered against the sons of the Children of Israel, while Ibn Jurayj understood it as the risk that the infant's crying would be heard by neighbours. The length of nursing is given as three, four or eight months. The yamm is, for most, the Nile.

As for the words "do not fear and do not grieve", Ibn Zayd and Ibn al-Jawzi understood fear as drowning and grief as separation, while Yahya ibn Sallam took fear as loss and grief as his being killed. Zamakhshari distinguishes fear, a distress over a future harm, from grief, a distress over a harm already occurred. The promise that God will return him and make him a messenger is the good news. Concerning the lam in "that he might be to them an enemy and a grief", most take it as the lam of outcome rather than purpose, though Ibn Kathir reads it as purpose in relation to God's knowledge.

This verse describes how Pharaoh's people picked up the infant Moses after his mother had set him adrift on the river, as she had been inspired to do. The commentators explain that the verb iltaqata means to come upon something without seeking it. They differ on who the 'family of Pharaoh' were: al-Tabari relays the views of as-Suddi and Ibn Ishaq that they were Pharaoh's wife's maidservants or his helpers, while Muhammad ibn Qays holds that it was Pharaoh's daughter, whose leprosy was cured by the infant's saliva. As for 'that it might be to them an enemy and a grief', most commentators, including az-Zamakhshari, Ibn Atiyya, al-Qurtubi and al-Baghawi, take the lam to be a lam of consequence: they did not pick him up for that purpose, but their end came to that. Ibn Kathir holds that it still carries a causal sense within God's decree, while Ibn al-Qayyim reports Ibn Taymiyya's objection to using this lam for God's acts. On the recitation, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read 'huznan' with a damma, the others 'hazanan'; both forms are considered equivalent in meaning. The commentators agree that Pharaoh, Haman and their armies were sinners and transgressors, and that this is why Moses became their adversary. They differ on the sense of 'khati'in': al-Hasan read it as heedlessness of their coming loss of rule, while most took it as disobedience and sin.

This verse records the words of Pharaoh's wife, Asiya daughter of Muzahim, when Pharaoh and his men wanted to kill the infant Moses. She says the child is a delight for her and for him, and asks that he not be killed, since he may benefit them or they may adopt him, while they do not perceive what will become of him. Commentators note that the infant whom Pharaoh's household took from the river, after his mother had placed him in the chest, thus entered the royal palace. Most hold that the lam in "that he might be to them an enemy and a grief" is the lam of outcome rather than purpose. All agree that Asiya spoke to secure his life; they differ on when she spoke. Ibn Abbas, Ibn Ishaq and al-Suddi place it at the moment he pulled Pharaoh's beard or when he was found, while others place it when Pharaoh decided to kill him. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir cite a hadith that had Pharaoh said as she did, God would have guided him, but he was denied this; the hadith's chain is discussed, and some read it as a hypothetical. On "and they perceive not", Qatada and Mujahid take it to mean they do not realise their ruin would come at his hands; Ibn Ishaq takes it to mean they do not realise that God does what He wills and not what they will; al-Kalbi takes it to mean they do not know he is of the Children of Israel. Al-Tabari concludes that the most sound reading is that Pharaoh and his people do not know their destruction would come through him, since this follows the preceding context most naturally.

The verse describes the state of Moses' mother after she had placed her child in the river: her heart became empty of everything except Moses, and she almost revealed the secret, nearly crying out that he was her son, but God strengthened her heart so that she would be among the believers, those who trust God's promise. Most commentators, including Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada, Mujahid, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Qurtubi, take the emptiness to mean free of all concern except for Moses. Al-Hasan, Ibn Ishaq and Ibn Zayd understand it as her forgetting the revealed promise and command, while Abu 'Ubayda and al-Akhfash read it as freedom from grief because she knew he would not drown; al-Qutayba and Ibn 'Atiyya reject this reading, since God's binding of her heart suits anguish rather than calm. Malik and others understand it as the loss of reason from shock. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi suggest that her heart was emptied of anxiety after she heard Pharaoh had adopted him. As for the pronoun in 'to reveal it', most, including Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada, al-Suddi and al-Tabari, refer it to Moses, so that she nearly cried out 'O my son'; others refer it to the revelation. Regarding 'binding upon her heart', commentators cite faith, divine protection or patience. The faith mentioned is a firm trust in God's promise to return him to her and make him a messenger.

This verse tells how Moses's mother asked his sister to follow the basket on the river and find out what happened to him. She watched him from a distance without approaching, and Pharaoh's people did not realise she was his sister or that she was following him. The commentators agree that "qusseehi" means follow his trace and seek news of him, and that "'an junub" means from afar. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir state this clearly, and al-Tabari supports it with a line of poetry. Ibn al-Jawzi, Abu Hayyan and Ibn Juzayy also report the meaning "out of longing", attributed to Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' and to the tribe of Judham, while Ibn 'Abbas understood it as from the side. Al-Sha'rawi notes that the word denotes distance, not nearness. Most exegetes, including al-Baghawi, al-Razi and al-Qurtubi, name the sister Maryam, though al-Qurtubi and al-Baydawi also mention Kalthama or Kulthum, and Ibn 'Uthaymin considers the name unsupported. The commentators stress her caution in not drawing attention to herself, which they see as both her own wisdom and God's care for Moses. The verse contains no legal ruling; it describes the discreet action of a sensible sister amid danger and prepares the account of Moses's return to his mother.

This passage tells how God prevented the infant Moses from accepting the breasts of any wet-nurse, so that Pharaoh's household was distressed. His sister, who had been following his fate, then offered to point them to a family that would nurse and raise him and would sincerely care for him. Most commentators, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi, take the words 'and they are sincere toward him' to refer to the child; when pressed about whether she knew the family, she said she meant that they were sincere toward the king. All agree on the outcome: the child was returned to his mother, her eye was comforted and her grief lifted, and she saw the promise of God fulfilled. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi and Ibn 'Ashur explain that the prohibition was a divine preventing of Moses from nursing, not a legal ruling. Ibn Kathir, al-Nasafi and al-Baghawi report that Pharaoh paid the mother a daily dinar, a narrative some modern commentators treat with caution. Then the commentators agree that Moses was raised in Pharaoh's household, reached maturity and was given wisdom and knowledge before his prophethood. Many, including Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi, view the killing of the Copt as an error for which Moses asked forgiveness, and it led to his flight to Madyan.

The commentators explain that this verse describes Moses being returned to his mother after God had prevented him from accepting the breasts of the wet-nurses. When Moses's sister offered the household of Pharaoh a family that could nurse and raise him, they agreed, and she brought the mother, whose breast he accepted. He was thus returned to her so that her eye would be comforted, that she would not grieve, and that she would know God's promise to be true. The scholars agree that this return fulfilled the divine promise. As to who does not know, al-Tabari, Qatada, Mujahid and Ibn Kathir take it to mean the many polytheists who do not believe God's promise, while al-Razi understands it as the people of Egypt in general. Al-Dahhak and Muqatil identify them as Pharaoh's household, who did not know that God had promised the mother her son's return. Ibn Atiyya, al-Baghawi and others report further details of the story, including that Moses refused the nurses for eight days. Al-Zamakhshari regards the payment the mother received as enemy property taken lawfully, whereas Ibn Atiyya treats it as a wage. Ibn Ashur explains the closing phrase as meaning that few people could see this evidence. Several commentators read the verse as a veiled reference to the mother's distress on hearing that her son had fallen into Pharaoh's hands; in their view, the main purpose of the return was her knowledge of God's truthful promise, with comforted eyes and relieved grief following from it.

This verse states that when Moses reached full bodily strength and maturity of mind, God gave him judgment and knowledge. The commentators broadly agree that this gift came before his prophethood, and that the reward mentioned at the end of the verse is the recompense granted to those who do good. The age of full strength and maturity, however, is disputed. Mujahid, Qatada and Ibn Zayd hold that maturity means forty years, while Ibn Abbas and Sa'id ibn Jubayr say full strength is thirty-three years. Al-Kalbi places it between eighteen and thirty, and al-Mawardi records a range of opinions from fifteen to forty years. Al-Zamakhshari understands maturity as the completion of reason and physique, and notes the tradition that no prophet was sent before forty. On the meaning of judgment and knowledge, Mujahid, Ibn Zayd and Ibn Ishaq explain them as understanding and religious knowledge, al-Sudi as prophethood, and al-Zamakhshari as the Torah and the Sunna. Ibn Kathir, al-Baydawi and Ibn Ashur favour wisdom and religious learning, arguing that prophethood cannot be a reward for deeds. Al-Razi separates bodily strength from intellectual maturity and holds that the two terms have distinct meanings.

This passage tells how Moses entered the city of Pharaoh, which some name Memphis or Ayn Shams, at a time when its people were unaware, namely the midday rest for most commentators. He found two men fighting: one was from his own people, the Israelites, and the other was a Copt from Pharaoh's people. The Israelite called on Moses for help against the Copt. Moses struck him with a closed fist and the man died, though according to most reports Moses did not intend to kill him. He then regretted it and said this was the work of Satan, who had stirred his anger, for Satan is a manifest and misleading enemy. The commentators agree that Moses did not intend to kill and that he asked God for forgiveness, but they differ on the city and the time. Al-Tabari and al-Baghawi identify the city as Memphis and the time as midday, while al-Zamakhshari and Ibn al-Jawzi report other views, such as the interval between sunset and the night prayer, or a festival day. On the identity of the two men, Ibn Abbas and Qatada say one was Israelite and the other Coptic, while al-Tha'labi and al-Razi mention that the Israelite may have been al-Samiri and the Copt a cook of Pharaoh. Al-Razi holds that the Israelite was a believer, whereas Muqatil says both were disbelievers. Most say the blow was struck with a clenched fist, though some say it was with a staff. Al-Hasan holds that killing a disbeliever was not lawful in that situation, and Ibn Jurayj reports that a prophet should not kill without a command. Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi relate that the dispute arose because the Copt had forced the Israelite to carry firewood for Pharaoh's kitchen, an account that some regard as sound and others as weak.

This verse records Moses' repentance after he struck the Egyptian who was beating an Israelite and the man died. The commentators explain that Moses said: "My Lord, I have wronged myself by killing this man without Your command; forgive me and do not punish me," and God forgave him, for He is the Forgiving, the Merciful. They agree that Moses did not intend to kill and only meant to push the aggressor away, and that the event occurred before his mission or before he was permitted to kill, which is why he calls it a wrong to himself. Ibn Kathir, al-Jalalayn and Abu al-Su'ud take the plea for forgiveness to concern the killing. Al-Razi and others explain that wronging oneself means forgoing a greater reward by leaving the preferable course, and al-Razi also suggests Moses asked that the matter be kept from Pharaoh. Ibn 'Ashur sees the passage as a simple confession that God accepted. Regarding the following words, in which Moses vows never to support the wrongdoers, Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Zamakhshari and al-Qurtubi draw a ruling against assisting oppressors, including serving them or writing for them, while al-Zamakhshari also reads it as a plea for protection. Al-Tabari reports the view of Ibn 'Abbas that Moses did not add "if God wills" and was then tested. The scholars agree on the meaning of forgiveness and repentance but differ on how to characterise the act and on the question of the prophets' infallibility, and none of them settles it.

The commentators explain that Moses, after God had forgiven him for killing the Copt, said in gratitude: "My Lord, for the favours You have bestowed upon me," meaning the forgiveness and other blessings, "I will never be a supporter of the criminals." Most agree that this is Moses' pledge to give thanks and to refrain from helping wrongdoers. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi take the criminals to be the disbelievers and polytheists, whereas al-Zamakhshari holds that supporting them may mean joining Pharaoh's entourage or aiding someone whose help leads to sin, as in the Israelite's quarrel that caused the killing. Al-Kisa'i and al-Farra' read the sentence as a supplication rather than a statement, while an-Nahhas finds the declarative reading more fitting to the context. Ibn Abbas reports that Moses did not add the exception "if God wills" and was afterwards tested, and Qatada calls it a lapse for the same reason. Ibn Atiyya and al-Qurtubi draw from the verse a prohibition on helping or serving oppressors, a view they attribute to Ata' ibn Abi Rabah. Ibn Ashur explains that the word zahir means helper and that Moses wished to express his gratitude for wisdom and knowledge by defending the truth. The commentators differ on the favour meant: forgiveness for some, guidance, prophethood, strength, or knowledge and wisdom for others, though all these readings point to the same lesson of refusing to support wrongdoers.

This verse describes Moses after he accidentally killed an Egyptian in the city. He stayed there in fear, watching for news and for what people would do to him. Suddenly the Israelite who had sought his help the day before called for help again against another Egyptian. Moses said to him, in reproach, that he was clearly misguided, since he was fighting again today as he had yesterday. The commentators agree on this general sense, that both istansara and istasrakha mean asking for help, and that Moses feared being held to account for the killing. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Ashur note that he dreaded his deed being discovered. They differ on who speaks next: al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Nasafi take Moses to be addressing the Israelite with the words "you are misguided", while al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Juzayy allow that they may be aimed at the Egyptian, though most hold they are for the Israelite. Al-Mawardi, Ibn al-Jawzi and Ibn Kathir report that it was the Israelite who, fearing a blow from Moses, answered "do you want to kill me as you killed a man yesterday?". Al-Razi, al-Qurtubi and Ibn 'Ashur argue that the Egyptian was the speaker, having learned the truth. Al-Qurtubi notes that "ghawi" may mean one who leads others astray or one who goes astray himself. As for "jabbar", al-Qurtubi and al-Mawardi define it as one who kills without right, and al-Zamakhshari as one who strikes and kills unjustly without weighing the consequences.

The commentators explain that Moses, having killed an Egyptian by mistake, repented and asked his Lord for forgiveness. The next morning he was in the city, fearful and watchful for news, when he saw the Israelite he had helped the day before calling out to him against another Egyptian. Moses told him he was clearly misguided. When he then moved to strike the Egyptian, the Israelite, thinking he was the target, said: "Do you want to kill me as you killed a man yesterday? You only want to be a tyrant in the land, and you do not want to be one of the reformers." Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Qurtubi agree that the tyrant is one who kills unjustly, and al-Sha'bi and Ikrima report that whoever kills two people without right is a tyrant. As to who spoke these words, most exegetes, including Ibn 'Abbas, al-Baghawi and Ibn al-Jawzi, attribute them to the Israelite. Others, such as al-Hasan, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Zamakhshari, allow that it may have been the Egyptian, while al-Alusi, Ibn 'Ashur and Ibn 'Uthaymin hold that it was the Egyptian who inferred that Moses was the killer. Commentators also differ on the meaning of "ghawiyy": one who misleads or one who is misguided. They agree on the general sense that reform stands opposed to violence. The incident spread until it reached Pharaoh and his chiefs, who plotted to kill Moses, but a man came to warn him to leave the city, and he left, fearful, asking his Lord to save him from the wrongdoing people.

The commentators relate that a man came running from the far end of the city to warn Moses that the notables of Pharaoh's people were conferring about killing him, and urged him to leave, declaring himself a sincere advisor. Most hold that this man was a believer from Pharaoh's household, perhaps a cousin of Pharaoh, though some think he was someone else; the names given include Hizqil, Shim'un, Sam'an and Shim'an. Al-Tabari, Ibn al-Jawzi and Ibn Kathir read ya'tamirun as "consult together", while al-Zajjaj and Ibn Qutayba take it as "order one another" to kill him, and Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Qurtubi prefer consultation. Several accounts say the Copt spread the news after overhearing the Israelite recall the killing of the day before, whereas al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir attribute the remark to the Israelite, which they deem the more common view. On yas'a, Ibn 'Atiyya and others describe brisk walking rather than running, while others speak of hastening. All agree that Moses left the city afraid and watchful of pursuit, and prayed that God save him from the wrongdoing people; al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir add that he set out without provisions. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi treat the lam in "lak" as a particle of clarification rather than a complement of "the advisors".

This verse describes Moses leaving the city of Pharaoh in fear, watching for pursuit because he feared being caught and punished for killing the Egyptian man, and then praying to his Lord to save him from the wrongdoing people. The commentators agree that the fear was of being pursued and facing retaliation after the killing. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi report that he left without provisions or a mount, and that God guided him on the road. Al-Tabari and Ibn al-Jawzi add that Pharaoh sent men to search for him, and that a man from Pharaoh's household warned him and advised him to leave. Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Qurtubi name this man differently, as Hizqil or Shamʿun. Most exegetes read the prayer as a plea made in helplessness to God alone. For most of them, the wrongdoing people are Pharaoh's people, who are called unjust for their polytheism and for wanting retaliation for an accidental killing. Ibn 'Ashur notes that the account shows how God chooses whom He wills and prepares the means for His purpose. Ibn Kathir sees in the episode the beginning of the fulfilment of God's promise to save Moses and to establish him in the land.

The commentators explain that Moses, leaving Egypt in fear of Pharaoh and his household, headed toward Madyan, the town of Shu'ayb, which lay outside Pharaoh's authority and about eight nights' journey from Egypt. Not knowing the way, he said: perhaps my Lord will guide me to the right path. The exegetes agree that he set out without provisions or a guide, trusting in his Lord, and that these words show his reliance on God. The precise meaning of sawa' as-sabil is debated: Mujahid took it to mean the road to Madyan, al-Hasan the path of guidance, and Ibn 'Atiyya preferred the latter as the more eloquent reading, while al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir understood it as the middle of the road to the destination. Several, including as-Suddi, Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn al-Jawzi, report that an angel on a horse guided him; az-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya describe the hardship of the journey, with Moses walking barefoot until the soles of his feet wore away. Ar-Razi and al-Qurtubi note the family link, since Madyan was a son of Abraham, which explains the choice of direction. On the word tilqa'a, most take it to mean toward or in the direction of, and Madyan is not declined because it is a place name. The majority hold that the verse teaches reliance on God in fear and need, and the legitimacy of supplication that makes one's condition known. Modern commentators such as Sayyid Qutb, Ibn 'Ashur and al-Sha'rawi stress that Moses was less aiming for Madyan itself than fleeing, and that the journey was a divine inspiration leading him to a place of refuge and preparation.

This passage tells how Moses, having reached the water of Madyan, a well from which the people watered their animals, found a large group of shepherds giving drink to their flocks, and, apart from them, two women holding back their sheep and waiting until the shepherds had withdrawn. He asked them what was the matter; they replied that they could not compete with the men and that their father was an old man unable to water the flock. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Baydawi keep to this plain sense of the scene. On the verb 'tadhudan', al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir take it to mean holding back or keeping off, and al-Tabari judges that holding back the sheep is the more correct reading, since the women's own answer that follows supports it. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya stress the women's modesty and reserve. As for their father, al-Qurtubi, al-Razi and Ibn Kathir report that most scholars identify him as Shu'ayb, while others take him to be a nephew of Shu'ayb or a righteous man; Sayyid Qutb and Ibn Sa'di lean toward the latter view. Al-Qurtubi and Ibn 'Ashur draw from the story the permissibility of a woman going out for her needs while observing modesty, and the principle that the law of earlier peoples binds us unless it is abrogated, a point on which scholars differ. The readings 'yasdura' and 'yusdira' differ slightly without changing the meaning. These commentaries cite no authentic prophetic hadith on the details of this scene.

This verse describes how Moses, after watering the flocks of the two young women who had been holding back until the shepherds left, withdrew to the shade of a tree and called on his Lord, saying that he was in need of whatever good God would send him. The commentators agree that this good means food: Moses had arrived without provisions after a long journey from Egypt and was so hungry that, by some reports, the green of the herbs he had eaten could be seen in his belly. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir report that he spoke loudly enough for the women to hear, as a hint that they should feed him. Al-Zamakhshari, Abu Hayyan and al-Alusi instead hold that it was an indirect allusion with no explicit request, while others read the words as thanks for blessings already received, such as deliverance, wisdom and status. The same sources name the women as the daughters of Shu'ayb, but the accounts of how Moses watered the flock vary: he is said to have pushed back the shepherds, or to have lifted alone a stone that ten men could hardly move. Al-Zamakhshari notes that the omitted object points to the act itself rather than to what was watered. Ibn 'Ashur stresses the modesty and dignity of the two women. Opinions differ on payment: some say Moses sought no wage, while others say he accepted a reward for a kindness. Whether rulings drawn from this story bind later law, where the commentators disagree, is left open.

This passage narrates Moses' meeting with the two daughters of the righteous man in Madyan after he had watered their flock. The reports relate that one of them came to him walking modestly, covering her face with the sleeve of her garment, as recounted from Umar and Ibn Abbas, and she conveyed her father's invitation to reward him for his kindness. Most commentators, including al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir, identify the father as the Prophet Shu'ayb, while others, such as al-Hasan and Abu 'Ubayda, say he was Shu'ayb's nephew or a pious man of his people, and they differ over the daughters' names and over which one came to Moses. Moses accepted the invitation. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi and al-Nasafi hold that he did not seek payment but wished to be blessed by meeting the elder and to benefit from his counsel, whereas others explain that he may have accepted a reward out of hunger and poverty. When Moses told him his story, the elder reassured him that Pharaoh and his people had no authority over the land of Madyan, so he was safe. The commentators agree on the lessons of the scene: modesty, courtesy in speech, moderation in gratitude, generous hospitality, and the protection of the weak.

One of the two daughters tells her father that the best man to hire is Moses, for he is strong in work and trustworthy. The commentators agree that the work in question is tending the flock, but that the phrase is a general principle: strength and trustworthiness are the two qualities needed in a hired worker. To illustrate this, al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and others report that Moses alone lifted a stone from the well that several men could not move, and that he lowered his gaze out of modesty toward the two women, asking them to walk behind him and guide him on the path. The reports on how many men were needed to lift the stone differ and no consensus is reached. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi note that the young woman speaks in a concise, almost proverbial formula. Opinions differ on the father's identity: most identify him as the prophet Shu'ayb, others as Yathrun, Shu'ayb's nephew, or a righteous man unrelated to him, and al-Tabari judges that this cannot be settled without reliable testimony. Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Qurtubi observe that the jurists debated whether a work performed for the bride's family can serve as dowry, and Abu Hanifa and Malik did not agree on this point. Ibn Kathir reports that the daughter was regarded as the wisest of the daughters, and the commentators agree on the general scope of the rule about hiring.

The old man of Madyan tells Moses that he wishes to marry him to one of his two daughters, on condition that Moses works as his shepherd for eight years, and that if Moses completes ten years, it will be out of his own goodwill. The commentators understand this as a proposal for a contract, and his promise of good conduct is made subject to God's will. Most identify the father as Shu'ayb, and the daughter Moses married as the younger, named Safurah, though others give different names and Ibn Abbas leaves the identity of the man open. Al-Hasan said the man was Shu'ayb's nephew, and others said the elder daughter was the one married. Moses states that the matter stands between them, that whichever term he fulfils he will not be wronged, and that God is witness. Most exegetes hold that he fulfilled the longer term, relying on a hadith from Abu Dharr and on incomplete transmissions, while some consider these reports weak. Jurists have drawn from the passage the permissibility of marriage in exchange for service and the guardian's right to offer his daughter, but most scholars note that a law from earlier revelation does not bind this community, and the schools differ on these points.

This passage of Moses' story records that after he watered the flock for the two women and took refuge with Shu'ayb, he answered the man's offer to marry him to one of his two daughters in return for pasturing his flock for eight years, or ten if he chose to complete them as a favour. Moses said that this agreement stands between them, that whichever term he fulfils, no one may wrong him by demanding more, and that God is witness and guarantor of what they have agreed. The commentators agree that these words confirm and seal the contract with God as witness. They differ on several details. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Razi hold that the man was Shu'ayb, while al-Hasan, al-Kalbi and Ibn Ishaq speak of another man of his people or of his nephew Thaghrun or Yathrun, and Ibn Kathir and al-Sa'di find no decisive proof either way. They also differ over the names of the daughters and which one was given in marriage: Ibn Ishaq names Safura and Liya, al-Kalbi names the younger, and most say the elder. As for the two terms, Ibn 'Abbas, Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Ibn Kathir report, on the basis of an authentic hadith, that Moses fulfilled the fuller and better of the two, while al-Tabari mentions ten years after the eight. Jurists draw rulings from this: Malik holds that a father may marry off his virgin daughter without her consent; al-Shafi'i takes from it the validity of a service contract as dowry, which several Malikis also allow, whereas Abu Hanifa rejects service by a free person as dowry; al-Qurtubi calls it disliked according to Malik but valid if it occurs. al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi note that these provisions belong to earlier law and do not bind us absolutely. The staff given to Moses is the subject of many reports from 'Ikrima, al-Sudi and others, and Ibn Kathir and others note that none of them is authenticated as coming from the Prophet.

The commentators explain that Moses, having completed the term agreed with his father-in-law Shu'ayb, set out toward Egypt with his family. On a cold night, having lost his way, he saw a fire on the side of Mount Tur and told his household to wait, hoping to bring back news of the road or a burning brand to warm them. They agree that the address is to his wife, that the jadhwa is a thick branch with fire in it or a live ember, and that istilā means warming oneself. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi report that the completed term was ten years, while al-Tabari and Ibn al-Jawzi cite Mujahid saying he stayed ten more years; Ibn 'Atiyya and Ibn Kathir consider this weak. On which daughter he married, many favour the younger, relying on transmitted reports, while others note the text does not specify. Al-Mawardi and al-Razi set out several views on the fire: some say it was a light of God that appeared in a tree, others a real flame, and they differ on the tree, whether it was a thorn bush, a nettle or a lote-tree. Ibn 'Ashur observes that the Quran does not say which term Moses completed, since that detail serves no purpose in the narrative. The commentators read the passage as showing God's care for Moses and the gradual shaping of his mission.

When Moses reached the fire, a call came to him from the right side of the valley, in the blessed place, from the tree: "O Moses, indeed I am Allah, Lord of the worlds." The commentators agree on the core meaning: God is calling Moses, and the place is blessed because God spoke there and commissioned him. They differ on the phrase "right side": al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir take it as Moses's right, while Ibn Atiyya and al-Baydawi note it may describe the valley or refer to blessing. On the tree's identity, al-Tabari and al-Baghawi report several views: a thorny ʿawsaj bush, a wild jujube, or an ʿulayq plant, with Ibn Mas'ud describing a green sumra tree and Ibn 'Abbas naming the ʿunnab. On how Moses heard the speech, al-Razi and Ibn Kathir hold that God spoke to him directly, whereas al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi report that the sound came from the tree by divine creation. Al-Hasan held it was a revelation rather than a dialogue, and al-Qurtubi and al-Alusi note that scholars did not agree on the precise nature of this hearing. The passage then turns to the staff, which becomes a swift serpent; Moses flees without looking back and is reassured. Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi explain that drawing the hand to the side means placing it against the chest to calm fear. Commentators see these two signs as proofs sent to Pharaoh and his chiefs.

God tells Moses to throw down his staff, and when it writhes and moves quickly like a jann, a small and very swift snake, Moses turns and flees without looking back. His Lord then calls him to come back and not to fear, for he is among those who are secure. The commentators agree on the overall sequence: the staff's transformation, Moses's terror, and his reassurance. On the creature itself, al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and Ibn al-Jawzi take the jann to be a small serpent because of its rapid motion, while al-Nasafi, al-Baydawi and Ibn Kathir describe a huge serpent in body that moved like a jann, and al-Sam'ani reports that it swallowed what lay around it. Al-Razi explains the flight as the shock of a sign contrary to custom, and al-Mawardi adds the fear of harm from the staff. Most accept the sense of fear in the phrase about the ardhab. On the phrase about being among the secure, al-Mawardi gives two readings, safety from fear or being among the messengers, and al-Razi infers from it that Moses was made a messenger by these words. Ibn 'Ashur notes that the verb is linked to what precedes and that the repetition of the call to calm serves to reassure him.

These verses record God's command to Moses to slip his hand into his garment so that it comes out white and luminous without any defect, and to draw his arm back against his side to still his fear. The commentators agree that the staff and the white hand are two proofs from God sent to Pharaoh and his chiefs, whom they describe as a deviant people who had strayed from obedience. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi explain that the janah means the hand or arm, and that drawing it to the body dispels fright; Ibn Kathir reports from Ibn Abbas and Mujahid that whoever is afraid and places his hand on his chest finds his fear lifted. Al-Tabari, Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Razi take rahb to mean the terror Moses felt at the serpent. Al-Zamakhshari offers two readings: either Moses was hiding his alarm by tucking his right hand under his left arm, or the phrase is a metaphor drawn from a bird folding its wings to show composure. He also mentions the view, which Ibn Atiyya and Abu Hayyan consider weakly attested, that rahb means a sleeve in the dialect of Himyar. The readers differ on the vowelling of rahb and on the doubling of the nun in fadhanika, which grammarians explain in several ways. The commentators leave these views side by side as acceptable readings and meanings without choosing between them.

Moses tells his Lord that he fears the people of Pharaoh because he killed one of them, and asks that his brother Aaron be sent with him, since Aaron is more eloquent, to serve as a helper who will confirm his words. The commentators explain that ridf means a helper or support, and some add that it can mean an extra addition. Under the jussive reading, Aaron would confirm Moses' words once sent, while under the nominative reading he would be a confirming supporter. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi and al-Alusi argue that this confirmation means clearly stating the truth, establishing the proof and refuting doubts, not merely saying 'you are right'; the act is ascribed to Aaron because he is its cause. Ibn Kathir and others relate that Moses had a speech impediment after the incident with the ember, whereas Ibn Uthaymin holds that it was a congenital defect. Regarding his fear of being called a liar, al-Tabari connects it to doubt that they would accept his message, and Ibn Ashur sees in it an indirect request for divine support. God answers by promising to strengthen his arm through his brother and to grant them a authority that will protect them. The commentators differ on how the phrase 'by Our signs' connects to the rest of the verse, but this difference is mostly grammatical.

The verse records Moses' plea to his Lord: he fears, having killed a man of Pharaoh's people, that they will kill him, and he says that his brother Aaron is more eloquent than he is. He therefore asks that Aaron be sent with him as a helper, a ridf, who will confirm his words. The commentators agree that the ridf is a supporter and aide. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Atiyya explain that two witnesses carry more weight with people than one. Al-Razi, al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Ashur add that confirmation does not mean Aaron saying "you are right", but that he will state the proof clearly, argue it and answer objections, and so give practical support to Moses' message. Al-Baydawi and Abu al-Su'ud see the same idea of an effective testimony. On the reading of "yusaddiqni", Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Qurtubi report that 'Asim and Hamza read it in the nominative, as a description of the helper, while the others read it in the jussive, as an answer to the request, and al-Tabari prefers the nominative. Abu Hayyan and others note that ridf may also be linked to the sense of increase. Several commentators, including Ibn Kathir, mention Israelite narratives about the cause of Moses' speech impediment, while noting their weakness.

God tells Moses that He will strengthen his arm through his brother Aaron, grant them an authority, and so Pharaoh and his people will not reach them with harm; Moses, Aaron and those who follow them will be the victors. The commentators agree that the arm (adud) stands for the strength of the hand, and that strengthening it means giving support and help. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and al-Nasafi link the phrase 'by Our signs' to the verb 'they will not reach' or to an implied 'go', while Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi also allow it to depend on 'the victors', or to be an oath. Ibn 'Ashur holds that the signs include both visible miracles and hidden protections. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir understand authority (sultan) as proof, whereas al-Zamakhshari and al-Alusi take it to mean dominance and power. Al-Razi explains that the staff's transformation into a serpent is what keeps harm away from them. Readers differ over whether the word 'ridan' is pronounced with a hamza, and the exegetes do not choose between these readings.

This verse describes how Moses came to Pharaoh and his chiefs with Our clear signs, which testify to the truth of his message. Their reply was that it was nothing but invented sorcery, and that they had never heard of such a thing among their earlier forefathers. The commentators agree that the signs are the staff and the hand. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir explain that what they had not heard of is the worship of God alone, while Abu al-Su'ud and al-Alusi take it as a denial that a prophetic claim had ever been made, and al-Alusi adds the possibility that they denied prophethood altogether. Al-Zamakhshari notes that "in our fathers' time" means in their era, and that no prior announcement of Moses had reached them. Ibn 'Ashur and al-Qasimi point out that Joseph had already brought clear proofs to their people, so their claim was false on this point. Al-Razi argues that the ignorance of earlier generations cannot serve as a proof once the evidence has been presented and rejected. Moses answers that his Lord knows best who brought the guidance from Him, and who will have the good final outcome in the abode, and that wrongdoers do not succeed. Al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi understand the abode as the future life, while al-Baghawi and al-Tabari take the wrongdoers to be the disbelievers. Ibn 'Uthaymin adds that the verse shows that the signs were clear and manifest, and that the claim of sorcery was a denial of their evident nature.

The Quran records Moses' reply to Pharaoh and his chiefs, who had called his signs sorcery and claimed they had never heard of such a thing from their forefathers. Moses said: My Lord knows best who has come with guidance from Him, and who will have the good final outcome of the abode; surely the wrongdoers do not prosper. The commentators agree that Moses did not respond with insult but left the judgment to God, who knows the true from the false. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Nasafi explain that God knows whom He has enabled to achieve the supreme success, that the good outcome is a good end accompanied by mercy and divine pleasure, and that the disbelievers, being wrongdoers, will not prosper. Al-Zamakhshari holds that the abode means this worldly life, whose true outcome is good, and he supports this with other verses; Ibn al-Munir, whom he quotes, objects that evil too can be attributed to its people by the particle of possession. Al-Baydawi and Abu al-Su'ud state that the abode is this world and its real outcome is Paradise. Ibn Kathir notes a reading without the conjunction, while the majority read with it; Ibn 'Ashur explains that both readings bring out the contrast between the two speeches. Al-Razi and Ibn 'Atiyya note that Moses threatens his opponents with a bad end. Al-Sa'di and al-Jaza'iri stress that Moses spoke gently, following the divine command to address Pharaoh kindly.

The Quran reports Pharaoh's words to his chiefs: he claims he knows of no god for them besides himself, then orders his minister Haman to fire clay into bricks and build him a high tower so he may climb up and look at the god of Moses, whom he considers a liar. The commentators agree that the phrase denies the existence of another god rather than merely denying knowledge of one, yet they differ on what this denial means. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir hold that Pharaoh was in fact denying the Creator and that his charge against Moses was a lie about divinity, while al-Razi argues that he claimed a divinity of rule and obedience rather than of creation, and that he held no proof of God's existence could be established. Al-Zamakhshari explains that denying knowledge amounts to denying the thing itself, and sees a feigned certainty in his words about Moses. On the tower, al-Tabari, al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Kathir report that it was built and then struck down by Gabriel, whereas Ibn Ashur notes that the Quran does not say it was built and others think it never was. Ibn Kathir sees the move as a way to discredit Moses before his people. Al-Razi points to the mocking tone of the phrase "the god of Moses", and al-Baydawi takes the tower as a pretext to appear to be seeking the truth.

The commentators explain that this verse describes the arrogance of Pharaoh and his armies in the land of Egypt, without right, and their assumption that they would never be returned to God after death or be raised for judgment. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Nasafi understand this arrogance as self-magnification and rebellion against the truth and the message, and see their denial of resurrection as the cause of their tyranny. Al-Zamakhshari stresses that true greatness belongs to God alone, citing the hadith qudsi about the cloak of greatness and the garment of majesty. Ibn 'Atiyya, Ibn al-Jawzi and Ibn Kathir discuss the drowning in the sea; Qatada identifies it as a sea called Isaf beyond Egypt, Wahb and al-Suddi place it near al-Qulzum, and Muqatil says it is the Nile, though the best-known view, according to Ibn al-Jawzi and Ibn 'Atiyya, is the first. Al-Razi and al-Zamakhshari say that the image of seizing them and casting them into the sea, like a handful of pebbles, belittles them despite their numbers. The commentators agree that the curse followed them in this world, that on the Day of Resurrection they will be among the despised, and that those who called others to the Fire were leaders in disbelief. On the word zanna, al-Tabari and al-Baghawi take it as supposition, while Ibn 'Ashur takes it as knowledge implied by their disbelief. On the reading, Nafi', Hamza and al-Kisa'i read the verb in the active voice, while the rest read it in the passive. Ibn Kathir and al-Sa'di conclude that whoever believes he will not be held to account allows himself injustice, and that the end of the wrongdoers is destruction.

The commentators explain that God seized Pharaoh and his armies and cast them into the sea, where they all drowned. The command to consider the end of the wrongdoers invites the reader to take a lesson from it. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Baydawi report that the seizure was a punishment for their arrogance, their wrongdoing and their denial of the resurrection, that nabadha means to throw or cast away, and that the one addressed by the command to look is the Prophet ﷺ, who is to warn his people. As for the sea, al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Atiyya place it beyond Egypt, near the Red Sea or the sea called al-Qulzum, while Muqatil identifies it with the Nile, a view that Ibn al-Jawzi and Ibn Atiyya consider weak. Nearly all the commentators note that the image of seizing and throwing into the sea is a figure of speech expressing contempt for troops who were numerous, as one would toss pebbles, according to al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi, al-Nasafi and al-Alusi. Ibn Ashur sees a metaphor that may also refer to the push given to their march toward the sea. Al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi take the lesson to be the ultimate loss of the wrongdoers, while Ibn Kathir links it to punishment in the hereafter.

The commentators explain that God made Pharaoh and his people leaders in disbelief, whom tyrants followed, and who called, by their words and deeds, to the things that lead to the Fire: polytheism, unbelief and sin. On the Day of Resurrection they will find no one to help them or to ward off the punishment. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir note that this leadership is not limited to verbal calling: it extends to those who keep following them in error after their death, and the curse pursues them in this world. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi and others, who understand the verb “made” as “named them”, “left them to be misguided” or “withheld divine support”, read the verse in light of the question of God's creation of good and evil; Ibn Kathir, al-Qurtubi and others reply that the verse is to be taken in its apparent sense, and that leadership in evil is established just as leadership in good is.

The exegetes agree that “not being helped” means not being protected from the punishment, and that “the curse” means distance, disgrace and an evil reputation. The “maqbuhin” are those who are removed and cast away. Ibn Abbas describes them as having blackened faces and bluish eyes, while Abu Ubayda and Ibn Kaysan take them to mean those who will be destroyed. Al-Qurtubi and al-Baydawi report that some understood the pronoun to refer to Pharaoh's chiefs, who led the people into error.

Ibn Kathir, al-Tabari and others cite, through Qatada and Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, that God did not destroy any people with a general punishment after the Torah was revealed, except the town turned into apes. Some infer from this that general destruction ended with the Torah, while others consider the matter open to debate. Accounts about Pharaoh's tower and Gabriel breaking it are also mentioned, but many commentators withhold judgement on their authenticity.

The commentators explain that this verse closes the account of Pharaoh and his army. God drowned them in the sea, and He had made them leaders in disbelief, calling their followers toward what leads to the Fire. He then made a curse follow them in this world, and on the Day of Resurrection they will be among the maqbuhin, meaning the banished and rejected from all good. Most agree that the curse means being driven away from mercy, and that believers curse them and mention them with contempt. Qatada and Ibn Kathir link it to the verse, 'They were followed by a curse in this world and on the Day of Resurrection' (11:99). Ibn 'Ashur sees it as a lasting curse decreed upon them. As for 'maqbuhin', Ibn 'Abbas, al-Kalbi and Muqatil take it to mean those whose faces are blackened and eyes bluish; Abu 'Ubayda and al-Akhfash read it as 'the destroyed', Ibn Bahr as 'the defeated', while al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi and Ibn 'Atiyya keep the sense of 'the rejected'. Ibn Jarir and others attach 'on the Day of Resurrection' to the preceding clause, as a further curse. On 'imams', Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Baydawi read them as models of error, while al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi debate whether 'made' means 'called' or 'named', a point tied to the theological dispute over the creation of evil, which they do not settle here. A report from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, cited by several exegetes, states that God no longer destroyed a nation with a general punishment after the Torah was revealed.

This verse states that God gave Moses the Book, the Torah, after He had destroyed the earlier generations, such as the people of Noah, 'Ad, Thamud, the people of Lot and the people of Madyan. The commentators agree that "insights for mankind" are lights by which hearts perceive truth from falsehood, that "guidance" is a pointing towards the right laws and paths, and that "mercy" is a blessing reached through acting upon it. The phrase "so that they may remember" means that they recall God's favours and give thanks. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir specify that "mankind" refers to the Children of Israel. Abu Sa'id al-Khudri is cited in a report that God destroyed no people with a general punishment from heaven or earth after the Torah was revealed, except the town whose people were turned into apes; Ibn Kathir takes this to mean the end of general punishments and the legislation of armed struggle. Al-Zamakhshari reads "la'alla" as a metaphor for intention, while al-Razi takes it as expressing purpose, and Ibn 'Ashur connects the verse to the reply to polytheists who said they had never heard of such things from their forefathers, noting that the sending of prophets after long intervals is an established fact. All agree that the Torah is guidance and mercy; only whether the guidance is restricted to those who act upon it divides some of them.

This verse states that the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ was not present on the western side of the mountain when God entrusted Moses with his mission, nor was he a witness to it. His knowledge of these events is therefore a revelation from God rather than an account he saw or learned from others. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi agree that the western side refers to the western part of the mountain or valley where Moses's appointment took place, and that the matter decreed to Moses was the prophetic mission or revelation. Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Biqa'i note that denying presence also implies denying testimony, which strengthens the argument for prophethood. The following verses, read the same way, say that the Prophet did not dwell among the people of Madyan and did not recite their stories before revelation. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir take the address to be directed at the Prophet. On the voice heard at the mountain, opinions differ: Qatada, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi say it was God calling Moses; Abu Hurayra, reported by al-Baghawi and al-Baydawi, says it was the call to the community of Muhammad, who answered from their fathers' loins. Al-Razi, Abu Hayyan and al-Alusi set out the grammatical difficulties and variant readings without deciding between them. Commentators see in the phrase 'a mercy from your Lord, so that you may warn a people to whom no warner came before you' the reason for sending him to the Arabs, and they note that this removes any excuse from them on the Day of Judgment.

This passage states that after Moses God brought forth many generations, and time lengthened over them until covenants were forgotten, knowledge faded and revelation ceased. It also says that the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ was not living among the people of Madyan to recite their stories, nor present when the command was given to Moses. The commentators conclude that he knew these events not by witnessing or hearing them but by divine revelation, which is both a mercy and a proof for mankind. All agree that this account confirms the truth of the prophetic mission. They differ, however, on what the pronoun in 'reciting Our signs to them' refers to: al-Tabari, Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Nasafi and Ibn Juzayy take it to mean the people of Madyan, so the Prophet did not stay among them to learn their history, while Ibn Kathir, al-Qasimi and Ibn 'Ashur take it to mean the Quraysh he addressed, to whom he recites what was revealed to him. Views also vary on the 'command' given to Moses: some say it is the mission to Pharaoh, others the Torah or Muhammad's mission, and al-Zamakhshari reads it as revelation. As for the verse 'so that you may warn a people to whom no warner came before you', the commentators apply it to Makkah and the Arabs, while discussing the interval of no messengers between Jesus and Muhammad. Several hadiths cited by al-Razi and others describe a call addressed to the community of Muhammad at Mount Sinai, but some commentators regarded these reports as weak or hesitated to rely on them.

This verse states that the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ was not present at the side of Mount Sinai when God called out to Moses, and did not witness those events. What he relates of them is therefore a revelation, given as a mercy from God to mankind. The commentators explain the plain sense: God sent His Prophet with the Qur'an to warn a people, the Quraysh and the Arabs, to whom no warner had come before him, so that they might take heed and be guided. They agree that the verse establishes the truth of his prophethood, since he reports unseen matters he could not have learned from anyone.

Opinions differ on the call mentioned. al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Nasafi take it to be God's call to Moses on the night of the divine conversation. Others, including al-Mawardi, al-Baghawi, al-Qurtubi and al-Razi, relate, on the authority of Abu Hurayra, Ibn Abbas and Wahb ibn Munabbih, that the call was addressed to the community of Muhammad while it was still in the loins of its ancestors; Ibn Kathir considers these reports in need of verification. Some readers read 'rahmatun' in the nominative, giving the sense 'it is a mercy'.

On the phrase 'a people to whom no warner had come before you', opinions also differ. al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi understand it as the interval between Jesus and Muhammad, about five hundred and fifty years. Ibn 'Ashur holds that the Arabs are meant, since after Ishmael no warner had come to them. The commentators do not decide between these readings.

This verse explains that God did not punish the Quraysh and others for their disbelief and misdeeds before sending them a messenger, lest they argue: 'Our Lord, why did You not send us a messenger so that we might follow Your signs and become believers?' Most commentators take the answer to the first 'lawla' to be omitted, meaning either 'We would have punished them at once' or 'We would not have sent you to them'. The sending of the Prophet ﷺ thus cuts off their excuse and establishes the proof against them. The 'misfortune' is generally explained as punishment and retribution, and 'what their hands have sent forth' as disbelief and sins; al-Zamakhshari explains the mention of the hands by the fact that most deeds are done with them. For the next verse, the commentators agree that their words 'Why was he not given the like of what Moses was given?' are an objection to the Qur'an, which was revealed all at once. Ibn Abbas and Mujahid take the two magicians to be Moses and Muhammad, while Mujahid and Sa'id ibn Jubayr take them to be Moses and Aaron. The reading 'siḥrān' is explained by Ibn Abbas and Ikrima as the Torah and the Qur'an, and by Qatada and al-Dahhak as the Gospel and the Qur'an. Al-Tabari prefers 'siḥrān' because the context speaks of the Book. Ibn Kathir and others draw from these verses the point that no one can produce a book like the scriptures. Al-Razi and al-Qadi find in them arguments on theological questions, while Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Ashur agree that evil deeds before the mission deserve punishment in this world, though God punishes only after the proof has been established.

This verse describes how, after the truth came from God through the Prophet ﷺ, the Meccan disbelievers demanded signs like those given to Moses, such as the staff and the white hand, or a Book sent down all at once. God replies that they had already rejected what was given to Moses. The commentators differ on who is addressed: al-Tabari, citing Mujahid and Ibn Zayd, holds that the Jews who had urged Quraysh to ask this question are meant, while al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya point to the Quraysh themselves or their forefathers. As for their words "two sorceries that back each other", Ibn 'Abbas and al-Hasan take it as Moses and Muhammad, Mujahid as Moses and Aaron, and Qatada as Jesus and Muhammad. Reading it as "two books of magic", Ibn 'Abbas and Ikrima mean the Torah and the Quran, while others mean the Torah and the Gospel. Al-Tabari prefers this reading for the sake of the context, and Ibn Kathir considers the Torah and the Quran the likelier sense, since the two are often paired in the Quran. God then commands His Prophet to challenge them to bring a Book better guided than both; failing that, they follow only their desires, and no one is more astray than one who follows his desire without guidance from God. Al-Razi and others draw from this that divine guidance is not limited to believers. The phrase "We have made the word reach them" is explained by many as the successive revelation of the Quran or the reporting of past peoples' histories, so that they may take heed.

This verse commands the Prophet ﷺ to challenge the disbelievers: let them bring a Book from God that gives more guidance than the Torah and the Qur'an, and he will follow it if they are truthful. It answers their objection, raised about the Qur'an, that he was not given what Moses was given. The commentators agree that this is a challenge that establishes their inability and shows that their rejection stems from desire. If they fail to respond, they are following their own whims, and no one is more astray than one who follows his desire without guidance from God, for God does not guide the wrongdoing people. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi identify the two books as the Torah and the Qur'an, and Ibn Kathir considers this the clearest reading since God often pairs these two scriptures. Al-Mawardi, Ibn Atiyya and al-Qurtubi record other identifications depending on the reading: Moses and Muhammad, Moses and Aaron, Jesus and Muhammad, the Torah and the Gospel, or the Gospel and the Qur'an. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and Abu al-Su'ud hold that the conditional particle serves irony and rebuke rather than doubt, since what is demanded is impossible. Ibn Ashur notes that the challenge demonstrates the Qur'an's inimitability, and that the verb istijaba means to respond. All of them see in the verse the point that rejecting the truth is stubbornness and desire, not the product of any evidence.

This passage from Surah al-Qasas shows that if the disbelievers cannot produce a book more guiding than the Torah and the Quran, then they are simply following their desires without any proof. The commentators read the verse as a challenge to those who rejected the Prophet ﷺ: let them bring a book from God more rightly guiding than these two scriptures, and the word 'istijaba' here means answering that challenge. They agree that whoever follows his desire without guidance from God is the most astray of people, and that God does not guide the wrongdoing people. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi identify the two books as the Torah and the Quran, while noting the variant readings 'sihran' and 'sahiran' and the different figures proposed, Moses and Muhammad or Moses and Aaron. Al-Razi explains the grammar of both readings. Al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi remind us that desire can sometimes coincide with truth, which is why the phrase 'without guidance from God' is added. Ibn Ashur holds that the straying of one who follows his desire is the gravest, since he abandons the examination of evidence. The next verse speaks of the word God caused to reach the polytheists so that they might take heed.

This verse from Surah al-Qasas says that God caused His word to reach the people, linking and following one part of the Quran with another, so that they might remember and take heed. The commentators differ on the meaning of the verb wassala. Mujahid, Ibn Abbas, as-Suddi and Ibn Uyayna take it to mean explaining or detailing, Abu Ubayda and al-Akhfash to mean completing, while the majority, including al-Tabari, Ibn Atiyya and al-Razi, understand that the Quran was sent down in successive parts, its promises, warnings, stories, lessons and admonitions following one another. Ibn Zayd links the affairs of this world with those of the Hereafter so closely that the listeners seem to witness the afterlife. Ibn Kathir and al-Tha'alibi report that the pronoun refers to the Quraysh, whereas others, relying on a report from Rifa'a al-Qurazi, say it refers to the Jews. Several scholars, including al-Razi and al-Zamakhshari, explain that revelation in stages answers the objection that the Quran should have come all at once, and that it helps reflection. The commentaries then connect the verse to the people of the Book who believe in the Quran and receive a double reward, which some present as evidence for the truth of the message.

This verse describes a group of People of the Book who believe in the Qur'an: they believe in it even before its revelation, because they find mention of the Prophet in their scriptures, and then accept it when it is recited to them, declaring it the truth from their Lord. The commentators agree that believers among the People of the Book are meant, but they differ on who they were. Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Muqatil and Ibn Jurayj, like most exegetes, understand them to be Jews and Christians who converted, and al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir name Ibn Salam and Salman among them. Qatada, Sa'id ibn Jubayr and al-Baghawi speak of some forty or seventy men from Abyssinia, Najran and Syria, while Rifa'a al-Qurazi reports that it concerned ten Jews. Some take the pronoun "bihi" to refer to the Prophet, others to the Qur'an; al-Tabari, al-Nasafi and Ibn 'Atiyya prefer the Qur'an. All agree that their reward is doubled for believing in their earlier scripture and then in the Qur'an, but they differ on the patience that earned it: perseverance in their former book and in following the Prophet according to Qatada and Ibn Zayd, faith before and after the mission according to al-Dahhak, or endurance under abuse according to Mujahid. The phrase "we were Muslims before it" is generally read as monotheism and as awaiting the Prophet announced in their books. No commentator decides between these readings.

This verse describes people of the Book who, when the Qur'an is recited to them, say: we believe in it, it is the truth from our Lord, and we were submitting to God before it came. The commentators take these to be the believers among the People of the Book, though they differ on who exactly they were. Qatada names Abdullah ibn Salam, Salman al-Farisi, Tamim al-Dari and al-Jarud; Muqatil speaks of forty people of the Gospel who came from Abyssinia with Ja'far ibn Abi Talib; Rifa'a al-Qurazi says they were ten, including himself; Mujahid mentions converts from the People of the Book who suffered harm. Al-Tabari explains that their faith was long-standing, since they had found mention of the Prophet in their scriptures, and he understands Islam here as belief in what earlier prophets brought. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi hold that Islam is the attribute of every monotheist who accepts revelation. Ibn Juzayy takes the pronoun to refer to the Qur'an. As for being given their reward twice, most commentators, including Ibn Kathir, al-Qurtubi and al-Razi, read it as a reward for belief in the earlier Book and for belief in the Qur'an, and Ibn Kathir cites the hadith of Abu Musa al-Ash'ari about three people who receive a double reward. Ibn Uthaymin notes that the double reward belongs to those who believed in both revelations.

This verse speaks of those given the Scripture before the Qur'an, the People of the Book who believed in the Prophet ﷺ, and says they will be given their reward twice, for believing in their earlier Book and then in the Qur'an, because of their steadfastness. The commentators read the word 'patience' in related ways: Qatada and Ibn Zayd take it as patience in holding to the earlier Book and following Muhammad ﷺ, al-Dahhak as believing in him before his mission and following him after it, while Mujahid takes it as patience under the abuse of those who harmed the converts. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi combine these readings. On 'they repel evil with good', Ibn Abbas and al-Nasafi explain it as obedience that repels disobedience, al-Mawardi and al-Baghawi as forgiveness of insults, and others such as Ibn Jubayr, Ibn Zayd and Ibn Salam as answering wrong with right, folly with knowledge; Ibn Kathir and Ibn Ashur develop this as gentle speech and pardon. On 'they spend from what We have provided', Ibn Abbas and Ibn Kathir understand the paying of zakat and voluntary charity, while Qatada speaks of giving from their earnings. Several commentators cite the hadith of Abu Musa al-Ash'ari about three people who receive their reward twice, one of them a believer from the People of the Book. The exegetes do not choose between these views and treat them as compatible.

This verse describes a group among the People of the Book who believed in the Qur'an. When they hear idle talk or abuse, they turn away from it and say: "To us our deeds, and to you your deeds. Peace be upon you. We do not seek the company of the ignorant." The commentators largely agree that this "peace" is a formula of parting and disengagement, not a greeting, and that the "ignorant" are the foolish or those who are ignorant of God and His religion. They differ on what "laghw" means: al-Tabari and Mujahid take it as insult and abuse, al-Dahhak as polytheism, and Ibn Zayd as what the Jews had altered in their scriptures about the description of the Prophet. As for "to us our deeds", some explain it as: to us our religion, to you yours; others as: to us our forbearance, to you your folly. Al-Zajjaj and al-Nahhas say this greeting came before the command to fight, and al-Nahhas and others consider it abrogated by the verse of the sword, while al-Razi holds that avoiding quarrel remains commendable even when fighting is obligatory. Ibn Kathir and al-Suyuti report that the passage may have been revealed about a delegation of Christians or Abyssinians who converted after hearing the Qur'an, though Ibn Kathir notes that its meaning is general.

God addresses His Prophet ﷺ, telling him that he cannot grant the guidance of inner conviction, which belongs to God alone, who guides whom He wills, and He knows best who is fit for it. Almost all the commentators report that the verse was revealed about Abu Talib, the Prophet's uncle, who refused to profess faith on his deathbed. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, Ibn al-Jawzi, al-Baghawi, al-Qurtubi and al-Baydawi cite the accounts of Abu Hurayra and Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab found in the two Sahihs, while al-Razi notes that the verse itself does not prove his disbelief. Qatada and Abu Rawq take the words « whom He wills » to refer to al-Abbas, while Mujahid explains that « those destined for guidance » means those for whom God has decreed guidance. Most scholars distinguish two kinds of guidance: the guidance of success, which God alone grants, and the guidance of showing the way, which the Prophet does perform, as al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi, Ibn Ashur, al-Shinqiti and Ibn Sa'di explain. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi see divine favours that bring the heart to acceptance, whereas al-Razi describes it as a light cast into the heart. Ibn al-Uthaymin prefers reading « whom you love » as the person himself rather than his guidance. The verse also belongs to a context where the Quraysh claim they fear being snatched from their land if they follow the guidance; God answers with the safe sanctuary to which the fruits of every thing are brought, and commentators trace their stubbornness to ignorance. Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu Hayyan also record the variant readings of the verb yujba.

This verse records the excuse of the Quraysh: they admit that what the Prophet ﷺ brings is true, but fear that if they follow him the Arabs will snatch them from their land. The commentators agree that God's reply reminds them of the blessing of the secure sanctuary, where blood may not be shed and to which the fruits of every thing are brought as provision from Him. Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Nasafi explain that the sanctuary was safe for its people because of the House's sanctity, while the Arabs raided one another outside it. Al-Qurtubi and Ibn 'Atiyya add that safety meant no fighting, capture or raiding there. Al-Zamakhshari notes that attributing safety to the people is literal, while attributing it to the sanctuary is figurative. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir report that the speaker was al-Harith ibn Nawfal, though other narrations speak of a group of Quraysh. The readers differ on whether 'yujbā' is read with ya or ta, with the majority reading ya as Tabari and Ibn 'Atiyya note. The exegetes conclude that most of them do not know that this provision comes from God, and that disbelief offers no protection: God destroyed towns that grew proud of their comfort, and He never destroys a community without first sending it a messenger and its people being wrongdoers.

This verse says that Allah destroyed many towns whose people grew arrogant over the comfort of their livelihood, failing to give thanks and so disbelieving in their Lord. Their dwellings were left empty, inhabited afterwards only briefly by passers-by, and Allah alone inherits all things. Most commentators connect the verse to the Meccans' fear that they would be snatched from their land if they followed the guidance. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Atiyya explain that batara means insolence and misuse of wealth, failing to honour God's right in it. They also agree that the grammatical construction of the word for livelihood involves dropping a preposition or treating it as an accusative of specification. Al-Razi, al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi discuss these options at length. On the exception 'except a little', al-Baghawi, Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Nasafi take it to mean a traveller stopping for a day or an hour, while Abu Hayyan and al-Alusi note it may refer to only part of the houses. Ibn 'Ashur reads the inheritance clause as a figure of speech for the complete desertion of these places. Al-Qasimi and Ibn Kathir stress that these ruins serve as a warning to those who see them.

This verse teaches that God does not destroy a town until He has sent to its mother city a messenger reciting His signs, and that destruction falls only on its wrongdoing inhabitants. The commentators, from al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir to al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi, al-Nasafi and Ibn 'Ashur, agree that wrongdoing here means associating partners with God, rejecting the messenger, and persisting in disbelief after the warning. They read this as God's established way, grounded in justice and mercy, by which proof is established before any punishment.

On the "mother of the towns", most identify Mecca, as Qatada, al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir report, and draw from this that the Prophet's mission reached all surrounding towns. Others, including al-Hasan, al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi and Ibn al-Jawzi, understand simply the greatest or chief town of the region, and Ibn 'Ashur notes that the capital gathers the notables and sets an example for the rest.

The following verses are disputed as to whom they address. Mujahid says they concern the Prophet and Abu Jahl, or Hamza, Ali and Abu Jahl according to Muhammad ibn Ka'b, while al-Suddi links them to 'Ammar and al-Walid ibn al-Mughira. Qatada, followed by al-Qushayri, al-Tha'labi and Ibn Kathir, takes the statement as general, applying to the believer and the disbeliever. Al-Razi and Ibn al-Qayyim draw from these passages the discussion of the fate of the children of polytheists.

Scholars also differ on the sense of "batirat" (exulting in one's comfort) and on the exception "except a little", which some restrict to passing travellers, while others take it as the lasting effect of sin.

In this verse God states that everything given to people of worldly means, such as wealth, children, enjoyments and adornment, is only a passing enjoyment that is used during life and then vanishes, whereas what is with God, the reward and Paradise, is better in itself and more lasting, since it never runs out. The commentators agree that the verse belittles the life of this world and urges people to prefer the hereafter, and that the rhetorical question is a rebuke to those who do not draw this comparison with their reason. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain that 'lasting' means it has no end, while Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Baydawi add that 'better' means the pleasure of the hereafter is pure of pain.
