Abu 'Amr reads the verb in the third person, 'ya'qilun', which Ibn Juzayy and al-Nasafi consider less forceful than the second-person reading 'ta'qilun' adopted by the majority, while al-Zamakhshari thinks the third-person form is more effective in admonition.

The following verses, read alongside this one, have led to differing views on who they concern. Mujahid and Ibn Jurayj relate them to the Prophet and Abu Jahl, Mujahid and Muhammad ibn Ka'b to Hamza, 'Ali and Abu Jahl, and al-Suddi to 'Ammar and al-Walid ibn al-Mughira, while Qatada, al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Qushayri hold that they speak generally of the believer and the disbeliever. All agree that 'those brought forth' means those brought forth for punishment, although Ibn 'Abbas understands it as those brought forth for judgement.

This part of the verse sets up a comparison between the one whom God has promised a good promise and who will surely meet it, and the one whom God has given the enjoyment of worldly life and who will then be brought forward on the Day of Resurrection among those summoned. The commentators understand the good promise to be Paradise, and meeting it to mean reaching it without doubt. The interrogative form rejects any equality between the two. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Nasafi take the 'muhdarin' to be those brought to the Fire or its punishment, whereas al-Mawardi gives the sense of those brought for recompense, and Ibn al-Jawzi reports both readings. Opinions differ on who is meant. Mujahid and Ibn Jurayj say it concerns the Prophet and Abu Jahl, Mujahid in another report adds Hamza and Ali, al-Suddi names Ammar and al-Walid ibn al-Mughira, while Qatada, al-Qushayri, al-Tha'labi and Ibn Kathir hold that it is general, applying to the believer and the disbeliever. Al-Zamakhshari explains that the first fa marks the denial of equality after the clear gap between worldly enjoyment and what is with God, the second marks causation, and thumma signals a difference in rank. Al-Razi and al-Baydawi stress that God's reward is pure and lasting, while worldly pleasures are mixed with troubles and pass quickly.

This verse depicts a scene of the Day of Judgment in which God calls out to the polytheists and asks them where are the partners they claimed for Him. The commentators read the question as a rebuke and humiliation, and they supply the two omitted objects of the verb to mean that you used to take them as My partners. They agree that the answer comes from the leaders of misguidance and the heads of disbelief, who say that they misled their followers just as they themselves had been misled, and then disown them and their worship, since the followers were in truth serving only their own desires. Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi note that the devils or the leaders dissociate themselves from those who obeyed them, in line with the verse stating that friends will be enemies to one another that Day. The idolaters are then told to call upon their partners for help, but these do not respond, and they see the punishment and wish they had been guided. The commentators also agree on God's question about how they answered the messengers: their proofs fail them and they cannot question one another. Mujahid and al-Dahhak take the tidings to mean the proofs, while as-Suddi takes them to mean news, and the absence of questioning is explained either as not asking about lineage, following Mujahid, or not asking about the proof, following al-Dahhak. The passage closes with hope for whoever repents, believes and does righteous deeds, and Ibn Kathir and others hold that the word perhaps coming from God is a certainty.

This passage depicts the Day of Resurrection, when God calls out to the polytheists and asks where the partners they claimed are. The leaders and instigators of disbelief, against whom the word of punishment has been fulfilled, answer that they led their followers astray just as they had themselves gone astray, and then they disown the worship of these followers, who in reality did not worship them but worshipped their own desires. The commentators agree that the leaders meant are the heads and chiefs of disbelief, and that the misguiding was by whispering and adornment rather than compulsion, so that the choice belongs to both the one who misleads and the one who is misled. Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and Ibn al-Jawzi note that the admission of misguidance and the disavowal of worship mean that on that day they disown one another, citing other verses in support. Al-Zamakhshari and those who follow him explain that repeating the verb to mislead serves emphasis and clarification, and that the kaf in 'as we were misled' qualifies an implied verbal noun. Abu Hayyan reports the reading 'ghawina' with a kasra, ascribed to Aban and some Syrian readers, which Ibn Khalawayh does not consider preferable. Al-Sha'rawi sees in their words the wish that their own fate and that of their followers be the same in loss. All agree that the objects of worship will be unable to help their worshippers that day, and that the disbelievers will see the punishment.

This verse describes what will be said to the polytheists on the Day of Resurrection: they will be told to call upon the partners they used to worship so that these may rescue them. They will call, but receive no answer, and will see the punishment, wishing they had been rightly guided. The commentators agree that the verse is a rebuke to the polytheists and a demonstration of the helplessness of what they worshipped. They differ on how to read the clause introduced by « law ». Al-Zajjaj, Ibn Kathir and many others hold that its answer is omitted (had they been guided, they would not have seen the punishment or would not have worshipped idols). Al-Tabari and al-Baydawi read « law » as expressing a wish: they wished they had been guided. Al-Zamakhshari takes it to mean that they would have found some stratagem to avert the punishment. Al-Razi argues that the answer is not omitted and offers several readings, including seeing with the heart, which he prefers because it avoids disrupting the structure of the verse.

Some exegetes, such as Ibn 'Uthaymin, explain that the command to call upon the partners is not a real obligation but a challenge meant to display their powerlessness. Al-Tabari and Ibn al-Jawzi attribute the pronoun in « and they saw » to those who called, al-Dahhak to both the callers and those called, and al-Alusi finds the apparent meaning to refer to the callers.

On « then the reports were blinded to them », Mujahid and Ibn Kathir explain that the proofs were hidden from them, while al-Suddi and al-Zajjaj understand the reports to have become blind to them, so that they find no answer. Mujahid adds that « they do not question one another » means they do not ask about lineages, al-Dahhak that they do not question one another about proof, and al-Farra' that they fall silent.

This verse describes how, on the Day of Resurrection, God will call out to the polytheists and ask them, in a tone of rebuke, what they answered the messengers. The commentators explain that the question concerns their response to the call to monotheism and to abandoning idols, and that 'the messengers' refers to all the prophets sent to the nations. Mujahid and Ibn Juraij take the answer to be the testimony that there is no god but God, while Ibn Kathir holds that it also covers acknowledging prophethood, as the servant is questioned in his grave. All agree that the polytheists will be unable to answer that day, because their proofs will be obscured and they will have no argument left. Al-Tabari adds that God gave them full warning in the world, so they have no excuse. On the phrase 'the news was blinded to them', Mujahid and Ibn Kathir read it as the proofs, al-Suddi and the Jalalayn as the reports, while al-Zamakhshari notes that even the prophets stammer when faced with such a question. On 'they do not question one another', Mujahid understands that they do not ask about lineage, al-Dahhak that they do not ask each other about the evidence, and al-Farra' that they fall silent at that moment. Ibn 'Ashur stresses that the question aims at confusion and disgrace rather than information, since the questioner already knows the answer.

The commentators explain that this verse describes the state of the polytheists on the Day of Resurrection when they are questioned about how they answered the messengers. Their proofs and excuses become obscure to them, so they have nothing to plead, and they do not ask one another. Most identify the word "al-anba'" here with the proofs and excuses, as Mujahid, Ibn Juraij, Qatada, al-Dahhak and Ibn Kathir do, while as-Suddi takes it to mean news; the difference in meaning is small. On the phrase "they do not question one another", the views are close: Mujahid says they do not ask each other about lineage and kinship, al-Dahhak that they do not ask one another about the proof, al-Farra' that they fall silent at that moment, and al-Mawardi and al-Qurtubi that no one asks another to bear some of his sins. Ibn 'Ashur holds that all are equal in their bewilderment, so no one asks anyone. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi note that even the prophets leave the knowledge of the answer to God on that terrifying day. The context is one of warning, and most commentators add that whoever repents, believes and does good deeds may hope to be among the successful. Many, such as Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Qurtubi, say that "perhaps" (‘asa) coming from God is binding, whereas Ibn 'Atiyya reads it as a hopeful expectation grounded in good assumption.

This verse holds that whoever repents from polytheism, believes and does righteous deeds may hope to be among the successful before God. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and Ibn al-Jawzi explain success as deliverance, prosperity and eternal residence in Paradise. Al-Tabari holds that God's 'perhaps' (ʿasā) is binding, a view shared by al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi, al-Nasafi and Abu al-Su'ud, who describe it as the noble manner of speech that implies certainty. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi also offer the reading that it expresses the repentant person's own hope, so that he should expect to succeed. Ibn 'Atiyya argues that 'asā primarily signals hope rather than obligation, citing another Quranic verse, though he notes that many scholars regard it as binding and calls this a good opinion of God's generosity. Ibn 'Abbas, as reported by Ibn Kathir, also treats it as binding. On the meaning of righteous deeds, al-Jaza'iri and al-Sa'di understand them as performing the obligations and avoiding sins, while Ibn 'Uthaymin adds that the deed must combine sincerity and following the Prophet's example, and that faith requires acceptance and submission and not mere assent. In its context, the commentators describe the Day of Judgment when God asks the polytheists about their partners, who disown them, and then about their answers to the messengers, for which they have no proof. Several note that the following verse on God's sole choosing responds to those who asked why the Quran was not sent to a great man of the two cities; al-Tabari and Ibn 'Atiyya read 'ma' there as a negation meaning the choice is not theirs, while others take it as an object of 'chooses'.

This verse from Surah al-Qasas affirms that God alone creates what He wills and chooses what He wills, and that no creature has any right of choice over Him; hence the words "they have no choice." The commentators differ on the grammatical role of "mā". Most, including al-Qurtubi, Ibn Kathir, al-Baydawi and al-Sa'di, read it as a negation and pause at "and chooses", so that choice belongs to God alone, citing a parallel formula in Surah al-Ahzab. Al-Tabari reads it as a relative pronoun, the object of "chooses", meaning that God chooses from among the messengers and laws what is good for people, and he rejects the negative reading as unsound; Ibn 'Atiyya partly follows him. As for the occasion of revelation, many scholars, among them al-Mawardi, al-Wahidi, Ibn al-Jawzi, al-Qurtubi and Ibn 'Ashur, link it to al-Walid ibn al-Mughira's remark that the Quran should have been sent to a great man of one of the two towns; the answer is that God chooses the messenger. Ibn al-Jawzi and others widen the meaning to every kind of choice, and Ibn 'Abbas reports that the polytheists set aside their best possessions for their idols. Ibn al-Qayyim explains that the choice meant is election and favour after creation, distinct from the general will. The passage closes by declaring God exalted above what they associate with Him, by affirming His knowledge of what hearts conceal and what people reveal, by praising Him in this life and the next, by His sole authority to judge, and by the return of all to Him. The preceding verses promise that the one who repents, believes and does good may hope for success, and several scholars regard God's "perhaps" (ʿasā) as a certainty.

The verse states that your Lord knows what the hearts of people conceal and what they make public. The commentators agree that this knowledge covers both hidden intentions and outward words and deeds, and that the word 'chests' stands for the heart, which contains these things. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi link the verse to a reply to the pagans, who found it strange that God would choose a messenger from among men: creation and choice belong to God alone. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi and Abu al-Su'ud explain that what is concealed refers to hostility and envy toward the Prophet, and what is displayed to the insults they directed at him, including their claim that someone else should have been chosen for prophethood. Ibn 'Atiyya stresses that God knows both the secret and the open. Al-Sha'rawi observes that the verse puts the secret before the open, while other passages reverse the order, and he draws a lesson about the completeness of divine knowledge. Al-Jalalayn and Ibn 'Uthaymin keep to the plain sense. The scholars do not disagree on the meaning of this verse itself. Their debate concerns the neighbouring verse, mainly whether the particle 'ma' there is a negation or a relative pronoun, a question that affects the sense of the preceding passage more than this one.

This verse states that God alone is the true deity, that to Him belongs praise in this world and the next, that to Him belongs judgment in all things, and that you will all be returned to Him. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir explain that God knows what hearts conceal and what people openly show, so His choice of whom to guide is made with full knowledge of every hidden matter. The commentators broadly agree that praise in the Hereafter will consist of the words of the people of Paradise, "Praise be to God who has removed sorrow from us" and "Praise be to God who has fulfilled His promise to us," as al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi, Abu Hayyan and Ibn 'Ashur report. Almost all affirm that judgment in both worlds belongs to God alone, and that the return to Him will occur at the resurrection.

The occasion of revelation is reported in different ways. Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn al-Jawzi mention people who set aside their best possessions for their idols. Muqatil, al-Baghawi and al-Razi see the verse as a reply to the words of al-Walid ibn al-Mughira or 'Urwa ibn Mas'ud: why was this Qur'an not sent down to a great man of either city? On the grammar, al-Tabari reads (ma) as a relative pronoun meaning "what", so that God chooses what is good for them, whereas Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Zajjaj read (ma) as a negation, meaning that creatures have no right to choose over God. Ibn Kathir considers this second reading the sounder one, and al-Qurtubi also supports it by citing parallel verses.

Some commentators, notably al-Qurtubi and al-Qasimi, also discuss the prayer of seeking guidance (istikhara) and the formula transmitted from the Prophet, which is a practical application rather than the core meaning of the verse.

In this verse, God shows, according to the commentators, that night and day are blessings that only the Creator can grant. The word « sarmad » means what is continuous and never ends. The plain sense is: if God made the night endless until the Day of Resurrection, what god other than Him could bring you light? Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Jalalayn agree on this direct meaning, which aims to convince the polytheists that the true God is the one who holds creation and governance, and that the idols have no share in it. Most take the question « which god » as a rebuke and a challenge, and « will you not listen? » as a call to listen with understanding and acceptance. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi explain why light is mentioned against night: the benefits of light are more numerous, hearing suits the night and sight suits the day. Ibn 'Ashur sees an argument from the alternation of opposites, since the permanence of either would lose the blessing of their succession. Ibn al-Qayyim and Ibn Kathir stress the element of grace: people rest at night and seek their livelihood by day. There is a linguistic debate between al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi, who treat the « m » in « sarmad » as an added letter (pattern fa'mal), and those who treat it as a root letter (fa'lal). On the reading of « bidiya'in », Ibn Kathir reads it with two hamzas, a reading Abu Hayyan considers weak according to what is reported. The commentaries draw no legal ruling from this verse.

This passage from Surat al-Qasas offers an argument for God's oneness based on the alternation of night and day. The commentators explain that God instructs His Prophet to ask the polytheists: if God made the day endless for you until the Day of Resurrection, what god other than God could bring you a night in which you rest? The word sarmad means lasting and continuous. The exegetes agree that the verse establishes that divinity belongs to God alone, since no one but Him can bring night or day, and that it reminds people of the blessing of rest at night and effort by day. On the difference between hearing and seeing in the endings of the two verses, al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi explain that hearing grasps in daylight what sight cannot, while night is linked to sight because its benefits are perceived by others. Ibn Kathir holds that endless day would exhaust bodies and endless night would weary souls. Ibn 'Ashur judges that the argument from two alternating opposites is stronger than one from the existence of only one of them. Ibn 'Uthaymin notes that the interrogative 'man' asks for specification and is a challenge made on the polytheists' own assumptions. These commentaries agree on the force of the argument and differ on rhetorical nuances and reasons, with no practical legal consequence. The next verse adds that God made night and day out of mercy, so that people may rest, seek His bounty and give thanks, before the scene shifts to the Day of Judgment when the associators are questioned about their partners.

The commentators explain that this verse recalls a favour of God to His servants: the alternation of night and day. He made the night dark so that people might rest in it and their bodies recover from the fatigue of work, and He made the day bright so that they might seek their livelihood in it by His bounty, the purpose being that they give thanks. Most exegetes read the verse as an instance of the figure known as laf wa nashr: resting refers to the night and seeking provision to the day. Al-Tabari suggests that the pronoun in 'in it' may refer to the night alone, with the day implied for the seeking, while many take it as referring to both. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi and Ibn 'Atiyya explain that light is mentioned against the night because its benefits are more numerous, which is why 'Do you not hear?' is paired with light and 'Do you not see?' with night. Ibn Kathir notes that a perpetual night would weary souls and a perpetual day would exhaust bodies, and Ibn Sa'di invites the reader to reflect on blessings by imagining their absence.

The following verses are read by most as a scene of the Last Day: God calls the polytheists and asks where their partners are, then brings forth from every community its witness, who is their prophet according to Qatada and Mujahid, and tells them to bring their proof. They then know that the truth belongs to God and that what they used to invent has vanished. Al-Tabari takes the witness as the prophet, Ibn Kathir as the messenger sent to each people, while others mention the prophets or the upright of each community.

The commentators agree that these verses affirm God's oneness and refute idolatry, even though they differ in grammatical and lexical detail.

This verse describes the Day of Judgment, when God calls out to the polytheists and asks where the partners they claimed for Him are. The commentators agree that the question is one of rebuke and humiliation, and al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi note that nothing provokes God's anger more than associating partners with Him, just as nothing pleases Him more than His unity. Al-Baydawi and al-Alusi offer two readings of the repeated call: one stresses the folly of their view, the other shows that their association rested on desire rather than any proof. Ibn Kathir and al-Tabari explain that the witness raised from each nation is its prophet, who testifies that he delivered the message, following Qatada and Mujahid. Al-Razi gives a broader reading, in which the witness may be any upholder of the truth in every age, including periods without a prophet. When God says, bring your proof, they have no answer and recognise that the truth belongs to God alone. Ibn Kathir, al-Qurtubi and Abu Hayyan note that this knowledge no longer benefits them at that point, but it establishes the proof against them. Ibn 'Ashur explains that the verb 'dalla' means that their false claims vanish from their minds and from the scene. The verse thus portrays both their humiliation and the collapse of every support they had placed in false gods.

This passage describes the Day of Judgment, when God asks the polytheists about the partners they claimed for Him, and then brings forth from every community a witness who testifies against it. Most commentators, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, Mujahid and Qatada, identify this witness as the prophet sent to that community, citing the verse "How, then, when We bring from every community a witness?" Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Razi widen the meaning: the witness may be just people or bearers of proof in every age, and al-Razi finds this view closer because it covers periods without a prophet. All agree that "burhan" means the proof or argument they are asked to produce. Their failure to produce it leads, according to al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baydawi, to the recognition that the truth belongs to God alone. Al-Tabari and Ibn 'Ashur note that this knowledge comes too late to help them, though it serves to establish the case against them. As for "and what they used to invent strayed from them", most explain it as the vanishing of what they fabricated in the world, Ibn 'Ashur reading it as the image of something that escapes the mind, and al-Zamakhshari comparing it to a lost object. No commentator draws a legal ruling from this passage.

The commentators report that Qarun belonged to the people of Moses, that is to the Children of Israel. Most say he was Moses' paternal cousin, Ibn Ishaq holds that he was his uncle, and others that he was a maternal cousin. He transgressed against his people through pride, self-exaltation and the abundance of his wealth. Some report that he lengthened his garments by a span, al-Dahhak takes his transgression to be disbelief, and others say he oppressed his people after Pharaoh had placed him over them. God gave him treasures so vast that the keys to his chests were too heavy for a band of strong men, whose number is given variously as three, forty or seventy. Most exegetes understand the keys to be the implements used to open the chests, while others take the word to mean the treasuries themselves. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain that the verb tanu'a means to weigh down and bend, whereas Abu 'Ubayda holds that the verse is inverted and that the group is what rises under the weight. His believing kinsmen advised him not to exult, since God does not love the arrogant who exult. The commentators agree that the verse calls him to seek the hereafter through his wealth by giving in charity and good works, not to forget his lawful share of this world, to do good as God has done good to him, and not to spread corruption in the land. Qarun replied that his wealth had been given to him on account of knowledge he possessed. God answered that peoples stronger and more numerous than he had been destroyed before him. Al-Tabari, al-Qurtubi and al-Baghawi relate the account of his being swallowed up with his house, while others pass over the details of this event.

In this verse, Qarun's advisers from his own people tell him to seek the Last Abode with what God has given him, meaning the Garden, by spending in obedience to God. They urge him not to forget his share of this world, which the commentators explain as enjoying what is lawful without excess, and to do good as God has done good to him, and not to seek corruption on earth through disobedience and oppression. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Qurtubi agree that the Last Abode is Paradise. On the phrase 'your share of this world', al-Tabari reports from Ibn Abbas and Mujahid that it means working in this life for the next, while al-Hasan and Qatada take it to mean enjoying what is lawful without neglecting it. Al-Qurtubi and Ibn 'Atiyya also mention, without endorsing it, the view that this share is the shroud. On the good to be done, al-Sam'ani and al-Baghawi understand it as obedience to God, while al-Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir stress kindness to the needy and to creatures. Corruption is read as oppression and disobedience by al-Tabari, and as harming people by Ibn Kathir. Several commentators, including Ibn Kathir and al-Jaza'iri, report Qarun's reply that his wealth came from his own knowledge, and God's response that earlier generations stronger and richer than him had been destroyed.

Qarun replies to those who admonish him that his wealth was given on account of a knowledge he possesses, as the commentators explain it. Most exegetes read his answer as arrogant and self-satisfied, and God answers him that he should have known that He destroyed earlier generations stronger and more numerous than he, so wealth is no proof of divine favour. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Qayyim take the phrase to mean that God gave him this wealth because He knew he deserved it, while al-Baghawi and al-Qurtubi understand a knowledge belonging to Qarun himself. The commentators differ on what that knowledge was: the Torah according to al-Razi and al-Zamakhshari, alchemy according to Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, reported by al-Baghawi, and knowledge of trade and farming according to al-Mawardi and Ibn Atiyya. Ibn Kathir considers the alchemy view weak because alchemy is false, whereas al-Alusi reports the scholars' long debate over its possibility without settling it. On the words that the wicked will not be questioned about their sins, al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir understand that they enter the Fire without reckoning, Mujahid that the angels recognise them by their marks, and al-Hasan that they are questioned only to rebuke them. Al-Razi and Ibn Juzayy reconcile this with other verses by distinguishing questioning for information from questioning for reproach.

The verse describes Qarun going out before his people in his most splendid adornment, and those who desire the worldly life wishing they had what he was given and calling him greatly fortunate. The commentators agree that this was a grand procession of clothing, mounts and attendants, but they differ on the details. Mujahid, al-Nakha'i, Qatada and Ibn Zayd mention red or saffron garments and decorated animals, while Muqatil and al-Tabari describe a white mule with a golden saddle, four thousand horsemen and three hundred maidservants. Al-Tabari and al-Qurtubi gather these reports without choosing among them, and al-Razi thinks it best to set them aside because they conflict. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi say that those who made the wish were Muslims who wanted ease in the way people naturally do, while Qatada sees it as a wish to draw closer to God through that wealth, and others hold they were disbelievers. Al-Mawardi and Ibn al-Jawzi explain al-hazz as portion, rank or good fortune. Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and Ibn 'Atiyya take the reply of the people of knowledge to mean God's reward in the hereafter for believers who do good, and al-Razi and al-Baydawi link the words "none receives it" to that statement or to righteous deeds, reserved for those who are patient in obedience and in restraint from desires.

The Qur'an tells how Qarun went out before his people in great splendour, and those who desired the life of this world wished they had what he had. Those given knowledge answered that the reward of God is better for one who believes and does righteous deeds, and that only the patient are granted this word. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, Ibn Atiyya and al-Baghawi take the pronoun in 'yulaqqaha' to refer to the saying of the scholars, while al-Razi, al-Baydawi and Abu al-Su'ud take it to refer to the reward, the Garden, or faith and good deeds. Most understand patience as steadfastness in obedience, restraint from desires, and detachment from worldly adornment. The commentators differ on the details of Qarun's display: al-Mawardi and al-Qurtubi cite several opinions about his garments and mounts, and Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi relate many reports about the sinking into the earth, which al-Razi considers conflicting, preferring to rely on the Qur'anic text alone. As for the reason for the sinking, Ibn Atiyya and al-Baghawi link it to his wrongdoing against Musa, while al-Razi and Abu Hayyan read the particle fa' as indicating causation. On the word 'weykaanna', grammarians differ: Khalil and Sibawayh take it as 'wayka' followed by 'anna', the Kufans as 'waylaka' with the lam dropped, and others as meaning 'do you not see'. The commentators agree that the story shows material wealth is no sign of God's pleasure, and that neglect of the Hereafter leads to ruin.

The commentators explain that God caused the earth to swallow Qarun and his house as a punishment for his arrogance, his rebellion and his hostility toward Moses. Neither his followers nor his wealth could help him, and he could not defend himself against God's punishment. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and Ibn al-Jawzi relate that the earth took him gradually, first to the feet, then the knees, the waist and the neck, before closing over him while he begged Moses for mercy and received no answer. Ibn Kathir notes that these are Israelite narrations he chooses to set aside, and al-Razi judges them of little benefit and inconsistent.

Most agree on the general meaning: the verse announces Qarun's ruin and the absence of any helper, and the phrase "al-muntasirin" refers to those who protect themselves from the punishment. The particle "fa" in "fakhasafna" indicates that the sinking followed closely his going out in splendour and the wish of those who longed to be like him, who afterwards regretted their wish. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and Abu al-Su'ud report that Qarun harassed Moses and tried to discredit him through a woman of ill repute, while Ibn Juzayy and Ibn Kathir stress more his pride and wealth.

On the readings of "lakhasafa" and on the meaning of "waykaann", the scholars differ, as Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu Hayyan show, but these points do not change the core meaning. The verse itself does not settle the details of the story, and each commentator reports them without deciding between the views.

The verse describes the regret of those who had wished the day before for Qarun's position. Having seen the earth swallow him and his home, they say, in wonder and warning, that God extends provision to whomever He wills among His servants and restricts it for whomever He wills: abundance is no proof of divine favour, nor scarcity a sign of wrath. They acknowledge that God's grace spared them, for otherwise they would have shared his fate. The commentators agree on this general sense but differ over the phrase "wa-kaannahu". Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Qatada take it to mean "do you not see that", a reading also attributed to Ibn Abbas and Abu 'Ubayda, while al-Farra' treats it as an expression of affirmation, like "do you not see God's handiwork?". Al-Khalil and Sibawayh regard "way" as an interjection of regret or astonishment separated from "ka'anna", a view al-Zamakhshari adopts. The Kufan grammarians, including al-Kisa'i and Abu 'Amr, hold it to be "woylaka, i'lam anna" with the verb understood. As for the reading "lakhusifa" in the passive, it is the majority reading, while Hafs and Ya'qub read "lakhasafa" in the active. For most exegetes the verse concludes that disbelievers do not prosper either in this world or in the next, and that Qarun's wealth was no mark of honour with God.

This verse states that the Last Abode, meaning Paradise and its blessings, is prepared for those who do not seek haughtiness on earth or corruption there, and that the good outcome belongs to the God-fearing. The commentators give the word 'exaltation' closely related senses. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn Jurayj take it as arrogance, tyranny and overbearing conduct, Ibn Jubayr as oppression, and al-Hasan as the pursuit of honour and rank with the powerful, while Muqatil and 'Ata' understand it as refusing faith and looking down on people. As for 'corruption', 'Ikrima and Muslim al-Batain explain it as taking people's wealth unjustly, Ibn Jurayj and Muqatil as acting in disobedience, al-Kalbi as calling people to worship other than God, and Yahya ibn Sallam as killing prophets and believers. Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Alusi observe that the promise is tied to not wanting these two things, not merely to doing them, which warns against even the inclination toward them. Ali, Fudayl and 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz are reported to have dwelt on this verse, Ali giving the example of someone pleased that his sandal strap is finer than another's. Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Qurtubi report that some assigned exaltation to Pharaoh and corruption to Qarun, a view others answer by saying the God-fearing are those who avoid their conduct. As for the good end, most commentators identify it as Paradise, while Yahya ibn Sallam understands it as reward. The commentaries place the verse within the story of Qarun and contrast a passing abode with an eternal one.

This verse states that whoever comes on the Day of Judgment with a good deed will have something better than it, while whoever comes with an evil deed will be repaid only with what they did. Al-Tabari explains the good deed as sincere monotheism and the evil deed as associating partners with God, a view Qatada shares, whereas Ibn Sa'di and others take the good deed to mean all that God commands and the evil deed all that He forbids. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi, Abu al-Su'ud and al-Baydawi understand the "better" reward as a multiplied recompense, since a good deed is rewarded at least tenfold, while an evil deed is repaid only with its equal; they present this as a sign of God's grace and justice. Ibn Kathir and Ibn Sa'di likewise stress this combination of favour and fairness. Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Baydawi allow that the good may come in this world or the next, and Ibn 'Ashur notes that the verb "come" points to standing before the reckoning, so that the final outcome matters.

The commentators agree that the verse follows on from the mention of the Hereafter reserved for those who seek neither exaltation nor corruption on earth, and for the God-fearing who will have the final outcome. They differ on the meaning of exaltation and corruption. Al-Hasan sees it as rank and honour that leads to oppression; Ibn Jurayj and al-Dahhak as pride and tyranny; Yahya ibn Salam as shirk; Muqatil as arrogance towards faith. For 'Ikrima and Muslim al-Bitin corruption is taking property unlawfully; for Ibn Jurayj and Muqatil it is committing sins; for al-Kalbi it is calling people to worship other than God.

Al-Mawardi, Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Razi record further readings of these terms. The reader can take away that the text emphasises reward according to intention and action.

The commentators explain that this verse addresses the Prophet ﷺ: the One who imposed the Qur'an upon him and its duties will bring him back to a 'return' (ma'ad), and they differ on its meaning. Most, including Mujahid, 'Ikrima, al-Hasan and al-Zuhri, take it to mean the Day of Resurrection, when he will be questioned about what he was entrusted with. Ibn 'Abbas, Sa'id ibn Jubayr and al-Suddi understand it as death, while Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, Mujahid and Abu Salih take it to mean Paradise. Several, including Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ikrima and al-Dahhak, report that the ma'ad is Mecca, and that the verse was revealed at al-Juhfa during the migration, when the Prophet longed for his birthplace and was promised his return as a victor. Al-Tabari prefers the sense of returning to a familiar place, namely a conquered Mecca, while noting that those who read it as Paradise refer either to his entry during the Night Journey or to Adam's departure from it, which his descendants are said to share. The following words, 'My Lord knows best who has brought guidance and who is in clear error', are for most a reply to the Meccan disbelievers who accused the Prophet of error, while for others they confirm the promise and warn the polytheists.

The commentators explain that this verse reminds the Prophet ﷺ of God's favour: he did not expect, before his mission, that the Book would be sent down to him, and it came only as a mercy from his Lord. He must therefore not be a helper to the disbelievers, nor let the polytheists turn him away from God's signs, but call to his Lord and not associate anything with Him. For the phrase 'He who imposed the Qur'an upon you will bring you back to a place of return (ma'ad)', most take it to mean that He sent down the Qur'an, or that He obliged the Prophet to act by it and convey it. As to the place of return, Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and 'Ikrima, in one report, say it is Mecca, to which the Prophet longed during his migration, and some report the verse was revealed at al-Juhfa; al-Hasan, al-Zuhri and Abu Sa'id al-Khudri take it to mean the Day of Resurrection or death, and others the Garden. On the exception 'except a mercy from your Lord', al-Farra' and his followers call it a disjunctive exception (meaning 'but'), while az-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi allow that it is connected to the general sense. The word 'zahir' means helper or supporter, and the prohibition warns against leaning toward the disbelievers. For 'everything will perish except His Face', Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and ath-Thawri say it means deeds done seeking His face, al-Dahhak says God Himself, and Abu 'Ubayda says His standing; Ibn Kathir regards the first two views as compatible. All agree that judgement belongs to God and that the return is to Him.

God instructs His Prophet ﷺ not to be turned away from God's verses after they have been revealed to him by the polytheists, to call people to the worship and oneness of his Lord, and not to be among the associators or lend them support. The commentators explain that although the address is directed to the Prophet ﷺ, its meaning concerns his followers, who must not side with the disbelievers or support them. Some, such as al-Zamakhshari, see the prohibition as a way of stirring up the Prophet's resolve against the disbelievers, while others hold that the prohibition must be understood differently, since he could not realistically be expected to do such a thing. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi report two main readings of the phrase that everything perishes except His face: according to al-Tabari, Mujahid and al-Dahhak it means God Himself, whereas al-Thawri and Abu al-'Aliya understand it as deeds done seeking His face. Abu 'Ubayda takes the face to mean standing or prestige, and al-Razi interprets perishing as being liable to annihilation rather than actual annihilation. Ibn Kathir adds that the word ma'ad may mean death, the Day of Resurrection, Mecca or Paradise, and that several of these views come close to one another. All agree that judgment belongs to God and that people will return to Him to be recompensed.

The verse is addressed in form to the Prophet ﷺ, but its intended audience is his community: do not call upon or worship any other deity alongside God, for there is no god but Him. Everything will perish except His face, that is, Himself; to Him belongs the judgment, and to Him you will be returned. The commentators agree on the core meaning: it affirms monotheism and refutes idolatry, and that judgment belongs to God alone in this world and the next, with the return to Him taking place on the Day of Resurrection. On the phrase "His face", they differ. Mujahid, al-Dahhak, Abu al-Aliya, and Ibn Abbas in one report, as well as al-Zamakhshari, Ibn Atiyya, Ibn Kathir, al-Qurtubi and al-Razi, take it as a figurative reference to God's essence. Sufyan al-Thawri, and Abu al-Aliya in another report, understand it to mean deeds done seeking God's face, supported by a line of poetry about seeking forgiveness. Abu Ubayda takes it to mean God's standing among people. Ibn Atiyya and Ibn Kathir observe that these readings can be reconciled. On perishing, al-Razi distinguishes annihilation from ceasing to be useful, and argues that every created thing is contingent and therefore liable to perish. Ibn Kathir cites the hadith of Labid that all but God is vain.
